prose_changes.old: The Communist-era persecution these movements faced ended with the fall of Communism across the Eastern bloc, including the dissolution of the Soviet Union in 1991; the movements themselves lived on. The samizdat these communities produced came to be recognized as among the best documentation anywhere of what religious persecution actually looks like from underneath — not martyrologies written afterwards but bulletins written that week, listing who had been taken and from where. The pattern of unregistered congregations refusing the state's terms is kin to what happened in China over the same decades, a real historical relation rather than a coincidence.

prose_changes.old: In November 1918 Tahupōtiki Wiremu Rātana had a vision in Aotearoa New Zealand, and a healing ministry began around him from that year. In 1925 the movement was established as an independent church, Te Haahi Rātana, and Rātana himself was known as the mangai, the mouthpiece — a role that appears in the church's own creed, prayers and hymns alongside the faithful angels. The movement was political as well as religious from early on: a delegation took a Treaty of Waitangi petition to London in 1924, an alliance with the Labour Party was formed after a meeting with Michael Joseph Savage in 1936, and by 1943 the movement held all four Māori parliamentary seats. Rātana died in 1939, and the church continued under the tumuaki who followed him. Other Pacific movements of a similar shape belong beside it, among them Silas Eto's Christian Fellowship Church in the Solomon Islands, from 1960.

prose_changes.old: In 2010 the culture was alive and its texts were in print. It gave a large part of English-speaking Protestantism a default way of reading the Bible and a default expectation about how history ends, carried more by study notes, charts and novels than by any pulpit. It had institutional anchors — Dallas Theological Seminary's doctrinal statement among them — but it never needed a denomination. It also produced its own opposition. The reading of the Bible as one story fulfilled in Jesus, carried elsewhere on this map, was in large part a reaction against the chart. By 2010 the scholarship on it was substantial, from Sandeen (1970) and Weber (1979) to Boyer's When Time Shall Be No More (1992). Hummel's study came later, in 2023.
